ConnectionStrings.//: Set via user secrets or environment variables. Never commit credentials (SOW 3 - Security). Locally: dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:DataIntelligenceDb" "<connection string>" --project src\DataIntelligence.Api
ConnectionStrings.//DataIntelligenceDbReadOnly: Optional. A login in the di_ai_readonly role - SELECT on analytics.* only, DENY on sec and ai - that the assistant executes generated SQL as. Leave empty on a Windows-authentication-only instance, where that role has no login to authenticate as; the assistant then reaches the same restricted principal with EXECUTE AS Assistant:ExecuteAsUser. It never falls back to this file's read-write connection.

Auth.//: Authentication and authorization (FR-9). SigningKey is never committed and the API will not start without it. Locally: dotnet user-secrets set "Auth:SigningKey" "<at least 32 characters>" --project src\DataIntelligence.Api. Generate one with: openssl rand -base64 48
Auth.//Issuer: Written into every token as 'iss' and required to match when one is presented. Only this API issues tokens for this platform, so the value is a label rather than a URL.
Auth.//TokenLifetimeMinutes: How long a token is accepted for. Eight hours - a working day, so an analyst signs in once in the morning. Affordable only because tokens are revocable: every request re-reads the account and compares its security stamp, so disabling someone or changing their password ends their session on the next call rather than eight hours later.
Auth.//SeedAdministrator: The bootstrap problem, and nothing else: accounts are created by administrators, and a fresh deployment has nobody who can create the first one. Set Email, DisplayName and Password (12+ characters) via user secrets, start the API once, sign in, change the password, then remove the setting. Ignored once any active administrator exists, so leaving it set does not overwrite anything - it just stops doing anything.

Assistant.//: ApiKey is never committed. A DeepSeek platform key (sk-...). Set it with: dotnet user-secrets set "Assistant:ApiKey" "<key>" --project src\DataIntelligence.Api
Assistant.//Model: GET https://api.deepseek.com/models lists what a key can reach: deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-pro. Note the id has no vendor prefix - 'deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash' is the OpenRouter spelling and is rejected here.
Assistant.//MaxOutputTokens: Analytical queries ('which month changed the most') nest three levels of derived table and run to several hundred tokens of SQL before the explanation begins. At 1024 the JSON wrapping them was truncated and the turn was recorded as RejectedUnreadableResponse - the tell is a completion count sitting exactly on this number. A ceiling, not a reservation: short answers still cost short-answer tokens.
Assistant.//ExecuteAsUser: Database user switched to before generated SQL runs, used when DataIntelligenceDbReadOnly is empty. Must belong to di_ai_readonly. Created by database-schema.sql section 6.
Assistant.//HistoryTurns: How many earlier exchanges of the session are carried into the prompt, so 'and the year before that?' can be resolved. 0 disables conversation memory.
Assistant.//VerbatimHistoryTurns: How many of those are replayed as their full statements; anything older is summarised to one line - the question, the views it read, and the values it was bound to. A replayed turn supplies the referent a follow-up needs AND demonstrates the output format, but only the first of those is still worth paying for by the sixth turn: a nested LAG query is several hundred tokens of SQL that every later question in the session pays for again, where its summary line is about a dozen. Set equal to HistoryTurns to replay everything.
Assistant.//MaxSummaryRows: The length at which a result is DESCRIBED to the model rather than listed for it. The user still sees every row either way. At or under this every row is handed over; over it the model gets min/max/mean per column computed across ALL the rows plus the five at each end. Accuracy first, tokens second: sending the first 60 of 400 is not a smaller version of the truth - asked how far SOFR moved over a year, a model shown 60 days answers for 60 days and the real high is in the months it never saw, while a statistic over the whole result is exact however long the series is. 60 is chosen against what these questions want: anything asking for a figure, an average or an extreme is aggregated by the query and returns a handful of rows, which are listed as always. The cost is a question that genuinely wants a long list read out ('every day SOFR was above 5%'), which now gets a count, a range and both ends. Raise it where that is the common question.
Assistant.//ReasoningEffort: Sent to the cloud gateway as reasoning_effort. 'none' turns the model's thinking off; empty omits the field. This was empty on the assumption that deepseek-v4-flash does not reason - measured against the live gateway, that was wrong. It reports completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens, and on one CPI question spent 147 of its 208 completion tokens thinking before writing a statement essentially identical to the one it produced with thinking off (54 completion tokens, and a shorter prompt too, since the gateway stops prepending its reasoning scaffolding). Completion tokens are the expensive half of a bill, so this cuts cost without cutting anything the answer needed - nothing here benefits from deliberation, since the question arrives with the schema, the rules and four worked examples in front of it and the reply is one statement in a fixed shape. Set back to empty for a gateway that rejects the parameter rather than ignoring it. The local equivalent is Local:ReasoningEffort, where it is not an economy but the difference between answering and not.
Assistant.//Local: The second model the assistant offers, picked per question ('model': 'Local' on /assistant/ask). A model served on the machine the API runs on: no key, no per-token cost, nothing leaving the box - and a small model writes worse SQL and refuses more often, which is the trade the user is making. Nothing here is a secret, so unlike ApiKey it is committed.

Local.//BaseUrl: Ollama's root. Its native API is served here and its OpenAI-compatible one under /v1/; Api below picks which is used, and a leftover trailing /v1/ is stripped rather than turned into a puzzling 404. Another server speaking /chat/completions (llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM) works by setting this, Model, and Api to OpenAi.
Local.//Api: Ollama (native /api/chat) or OpenAi (/chat/completions). Native is the default for one reason and it is not preference: it is the only one that lets this application set the context window - see ContextTokens. The OpenAI-compatible endpoint accepts the same field and silently ignores it, which was tried and measured.
Local.//ContextTokens: THE setting that decides whether the local model works. Ollama loads a model at 4096 tokens by default and the schema prompt alone is ~3,900, leaving ~200 for the reply: anything longer is cut off mid-JSON, will not parse, and is recorded as RejectedUnreadableResponse after the full multi-minute wait. Measured on one question and one model, changing only this: at 4096 the reply stopped on length with the token total pinned at exactly 4096 and would not parse; at 16384 it finished and parsed. Sent as options.num_ctx on the native API. On Api=OpenAi it cannot be sent at all and must be set on the server instead (OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH); verify either way with 'ollama ps', whose CONTEXT column must not read 4096. Raising it costs memory, as the KV cache is sized from it.
Local.//Model: As the local server names it, tag included: 'qwen3.5' and 'qwen3.5:4b' are different requests, and a name that has not been pulled is a 404 rather than a fallback. 'ollama list' shows what is there; 'ollama pull qwen3.5:4b' puts it there. Raised from qwen3.5:2b, which could not resolve a date the question stated - asked 'what is the cpi in june 2025' it queried the current month, and did so against this prompt, against the longer one that preceded it, and against one carrying an explicit rule that a named period is absolute (that third produced a range starting after it ended). The 4B model, same prompt and question, wrote ReferenceDate = @month with @month = '2025-06-01'. It matters more than the size difference suggests: a query for the wrong period returns nothing, and nothing then gets explained as though the platform did not hold the data. 4B is slower per question and holds more in memory, both felt on a CPU - set this back to qwen3.5:2b where that matters more than the answer.
Local.//ApiKey: Ollama authenticates nothing and ignores this. Kept non-empty because some OpenAI-compatible servers reject a request carrying no Authorization header at all; empty it and the header is omitted rather than sent blank.
Local.//ReasoningEffort: Only used when Api is OpenAi; the native API turns thinking off with its own 'think: false' instead. Not a tuning knob either way - without it this option does not work at all. qwen3.5:2b reasons by default, Ollama returns that reasoning in a separate field while 'content' stays empty, and a 2B model on a CPU spends the entire token budget deliberating and stops on length with nothing in content. Measured here: 3+ minutes and nothing with thinking on, 18 seconds and correct JSON with it off. Note this is the field that works on /v1 - chat_template_kwargs enable_thinking, which the Qwen docs suggest, is accepted by Ollama and has no effect. Empty to omit it, for a local model that does not reason. Never sent to the cloud gateway.
Local.//RequestTimeoutSeconds: 0 means NO LIMIT, and that is the default. No ceiling was the right one: a 2B model writing SQL on a CPU is slow, the first call after startup also pays to load the weights, and how long that takes depends on the machine, its load, and how much schema context the prompt carries. 120 seconds was tried and ordinary questions ran past it - and a question killed at the deadline costs the whole wait and returns nothing, which is strictly worse than waiting longer for an answer. Not actually forever: the HTTP request's own cancellation still applies, so a caller who gives up takes the model call with them. The cloud gateway keeps its 30s - a remote call that hangs is a network fault worth abandoning, a local one is a slow machine worth waiting for.
Local.//MaxOutputTokens: Omitted entirely unless set, leaving the ceiling to the local server. Overrides Assistant:MaxOutputTokens for this provider only: that setting bounds what a metered API is asked to produce, and nothing here is metered. A cap only buys a way to fail - hitting it truncates the JSON wrapping the SQL rather than the SQL, so the reply arrives unparseable and is recorded RejectedUnreadableResponse after the full wait. A small model is the one most likely to need the headroom, being the one that rambles before it answers.
